readme: chaos-states — a note is a timbre, not a pitch. 96bpm, 16-beat loop.
chaossynth is a recreation of a Max/MSP patch: two sine oscillators, each
driven through an atan saturator into a resonant lowpass, and cross-wired
into each other. Two feedback loops make it chaotic. The inner one is per
voice — each filter's cutoff is driven by how loud that voice's own output
is, so getting louder closes the filter, which makes it quieter, which
opens it again. The outer one is between the voices — each oscillator's
pitch is bent at audio rate by the other's filtered output, so neither has
a pitch of its own for more than an instant.
Ten 0..1 control points steer it, five per voice:
a_cross  how hard the OTHER voice bends this one's pitch (the chaos knob)
a_drive  gain into the saturator, 0..50dB
a_pitch  base pitch, 0..1 mapped onto MIDI 0..69
a_res    filter resonance
a_track  how much the voice's own loudness closes its filter
and b_cross / b_drive / b_pitch / b_res / b_track for voice B. Voice A is
the left channel, voice B the right. /drone output=a to hear one alone.
THE POINT OF THIS SESSION. `seed` builds one configuration of all ten
inputs per MIDI note, 0 to 127. Playing note 60 selects configuration 60 —
every time, in every session that shares the seed. So a MIDI note is a
*state*, and any generator that emits notes becomes a way to sequence
timbres instead of a melody.
`spread` decides how far a note may pull the ten params you set by hand:
0 means not at all (every note identical — the params are the whole sound),
1 means the seeded state outright (the params stop mattering). In between,
your params are the centre and the seed decides how each note departs.
The three tracks here are that dial at three settings.
riff    spread=0.6, ten hand-written notes. Same rhythm every bar, but
each note is a different sound — and note 36, which comes round
three times, is the SAME sound each time. That repetition is the
whole idea: chaotic, not random.
flux    spread=0.95, driven by `roll` (randomnotes). Never repeats and
never resembles itself. The instrument with its lid off.
drone   spread=0, four long notes a bar. The seed is switched off, so the
ten params ARE the sound — every note would be identical, except
that two LFOs ride a_cross and b_track. A chaossynth param is read
once, when the note starts (the rendering is JS, so there is no
AudioParam to modulate mid-note), so the LFOs move the drone note
by note rather than sliding: four different sounds a bar, walking.
pulse   percsampler + `grid` (euclidpercs), so there's a floor to hang
the rest on.
Try:
/start
/riff                     the resolved state of note 60, and the seed
/riff seed=random         a whole new instrument, same notes
/riff seed=7              and back — seeds are reproducible
/riff spread=0 8b         collapse to one sound; the riff loses its shape
/riff spread=1 8b         and past your params entirely
/riff a_cross=0.5 4b      more coupling: pitch stops meaning anything
/riff a_cross=0.02 4b     almost decoupled — two clean drones
/riff a_track=0 4b        kill the inner loop; filter stays wide open
/riff a_res=0.95          and now it rings
/riff pitch_track=1 8b    make the notes behave like notes again
/riff random              re-roll all ten control points at once
/drone output=a           voice A only, both channels
/drone output=b           voice B only — the two halves are very different
/drone output=stereo
/flux stop                lose the wild one
/roll probability=0.9     more of it
The track is called `riff` and not `states` because `/states` is already a
command (it lists saved states). The engine renames a colliding object to
`states_2` on creation, and a session file that does it will not finish
loading — its own sends and patches then refer to a name nothing has.
pitch_track is 0 on every track here, so a note is purely an index. Raise
it and the note is *also* added to both voices' base pitch in semitones —
at 1, note 69 puts an uncoupled voice at A440 and melodic material reads as
melodic. Half measures work: 0.3 is enough that a rising line rises.
Events use `pitch` rather than `degree` on purpose. A degree is resolved
against /harmony, and shifting the root would silently renumber every state
— fine when a note means pitch, confusing when it means which sound. Patched
generators still resolve degrees normally, which is what makes `roll` walk
its scale through the state table.
Each note renders its own buffer in JS (both feedback loops are single
sample, which no Web Audio node graph can express), so notes are capped at
8 seconds and a dense chord of long notes is the one way to make this
expensive. `drone` holds 4 beats = 2.5s, comfortably inside that.
master runs a goodenizer called 'glue'. This instrument's output level
swings a lot between states — that's the compressor's job here, not a
polish pass. /glue mix=0 to hear how much it's doing.
